note: Attacker-controlled JS source bytes are copied into std::string s and passed to the Hermes runtime for evaluation; this is the entry point of the untrusted input.
The JS source is compiled to bytecode and executed; the program contains new RegExp("<32 spaces>\\") which constructs a RegExp whose pattern ends with a lone backslash.

code: auto regExpRes = regExpConstructorInternal(runtime, pattern, flags, false);
note: Executing new RegExp(...) invokes the native RegExp constructor with the attacker-supplied pattern string.
The constructor forwards the pattern to regExpInitialize to build the RegExp object.

code: return JSRegExp::initialize(selfHandle, runtime, pattern, flags, bytecode);
note: regExpInitialize calls JSRegExp::initialize with the pattern string that ends in a backslash.
The pattern (32 spaces + backslash, 33 chars) is appended into the stack-allocated SmallVector<char16_t,16> patternText16, which grows to a heap buffer; the trailing backslash is the last element.
The Regex object is constructed over the pattern buffer; its parser iterators current_/end_ point into this buffer, with end_ at the position after the trailing backslash.
Regex::parse invokes the parser over the pattern range, starting the recursive-descent parse of the regex grammar.
performParse begins parsing the disjunction; current_ is positioned at the start of the pattern.
consumeDisjunction loops while current_ != end_ and calls consumeTerm for each term; the trailing backslash is consumed as a term.

After consume('\\') advances current_ past the backslash, current_ == end_ (one past the last element). Dereferencing *current_ reads 2 bytes (char16_t) past the end of the pattern buffer, causing the stack/heap-buffer-overflow READ 2 reported by ASAN.
